mcqs.question: Which of the following statements shows a common misconception when trying to create groups of objects using only one property?

options.A: Grouping all magnetic objects together, even if some are metal and some are plastic.
options.B: Grouping objects that are the same colour together, even though some are metal and some are wood.
options.C: Grouping all transparent objects together, ignoring whether they are glass or plastic.
options.D: Grouping objects that are heavy together, regardless of their material type.

mcqs.answer: Grouping objects that are the same colour together, even though some are metal and some are wood.
mcqs.explanation: Option B reflects the misconception that colour alone can determine a material’s group. Colour is a visual property, not a material property like magnetism or density, so using it alone can place metal and wood in the same group incorrectly. Options A, C and D each use a single material‑related property (magnetism, transparency, weight) which is a valid way to form a group based on one property.

mcqs.learning_point: Creating groups using more than one property
mcqs.question: A student wants to sort a collection of objects using more than one property. Which of the following groupings correctly applies two properties?

options.C: Objects that are both magnetic and metal.
options.D: Objects that are either heavy or transparent.

mcqs.answer: Objects that are both magnetic and metal.
mcqs.explanation: Option C uses two properties—magnetism and being metal—to create a more specific group. Options A and B rely on a single property (colour or material type). Option D mixes the properties with an ‘or’, which does not require both properties simultaneously, so it does not demonstrate the use of more than one property together.

mcqs.learning_point: Explaining why a material belongs to a group
mcqs.question: Which explanation correctly justifies why copper is placed in the group of good conductors while wood is placed in the group of insulators?

options.A: Copper conducts electricity because it is shiny, while wood does not because it is brown.
options.B: Copper has free electrons that allow electric current to flow, whereas wood’s molecular structure does not allow free movement of electrons.
options.C: Copper is heavier than wood, so it conducts better; wood is lighter, so it insulates.
options.D: Copper is found underground and wood is from trees, which determines their conductivity.

mcqs.answer: Copper has free electrons that allow electric current to flow, whereas wood’s molecular structure does not allow free movement of electrons.
mcqs.explanation: Option B correctly identifies the underlying reason: the presence of free electrons in metals like copper enables easy flow of electric current, while wood’s structure lacks such free charge carriers, making it an insulator. Options A, C, and D refer to colour, weight, or origin, which are unrelated to electrical conductivity.

mcqs.learning_point: Using classification to identify suitable materials
mcqs.question: A kitchen utensil needs to be made from a material that is both non‑magnetic and does not rust when exposed to water. Which material from the list below would be most suitable based on classification of properties?
mcqs.explanation: Aluminum is non‑magnetic and forms a protective oxide layer that prevents rusting, making it ideal for the described utensil. Iron rusts, stainless steel can be magnetic depending on the alloy, and copper, while non‑magnetic, can develop a green patina (corrosion) over time. Hence, option C best satisfies both required properties.

mcqs.question: When classifying materials, what is the first step a student should take?

options.A: List all possible uses of the material
options.B: Choose a property (e.g., magnetism, transparency) that will be used for classification
options.C: Measure the weight of each item
options.D: Draw a picture of each material

mcqs.answer: Choose a property (e.g., magnetism, transparency) that will be used for classification
mcqs.explanation: The initial step in classification is to decide which observable property will serve as the basis for grouping. Without selecting a property, the student cannot form meaningful groups. The other options are later activities or unrelated to the classification process.

mcqs.question: Which of the following is an example of creating groups using only one property?

options.A: Grouping objects that are both heavy and magnetic
options.C: Grouping objects that are heavy and transparent
options.D: Grouping objects that are magnetic and conduct electricity

mcqs.explanation: Option B groups items solely on the basis of transparency, a single property. Options A, C, and D each involve two properties, which goes beyond the requirement of using only one property.

mcqs.learning_point: Creating groups using more than one property
mcqs.question: How does grouping materials using more than one property differ from using only one property?

options.B: It considers two or more characteristics at the same time to form more specific groups
options.C: It ignores the properties of the materials
options.D: It only uses colour as the property

mcqs.answer: It considers two or more characteristics at the same time to form more specific groups
mcqs.explanation: Using multiple properties narrows down the classification, producing more precise groups (e.g., magnetic + metal). Option A is incorrect because groups become smaller, not larger. Options C and D misrepresent the process entirely.

mcqs.learning_point: Explaining why a material belongs to a group
mcqs.question: A child wants to put together a set of objects that will float on water. Which explanation correctly shows why a wooden block belongs to this group?

options.B: Because wood is less dense than water

mcqs.answer: Because wood is less dense than water
mcqs.explanation: Objects float when their density is lower than that of water. Wood’s density is less than water’s, so it floats. Options A, C, and D give unrelated reasons that do not affect buoyancy.
